3. Discord between the Petitioner and Respondent No. 2 led to the Respondent No.2 initiating Petition Case No. 3566 of 2000 under Section 107 of the Code of Criminal Procedure on 24.8.2000 in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka against the Petitioner. However, by a compromise deed executed between the Petitioner and the Respondent No.2 on 18.10.2000 (Annexure-A') it was agreed among other things that neither party would interfere in the affairs of the other while continuing to live separately and that the First Party to the Deed i.e. Respondent No.2 would at her own initiative withdraw the Case No. 3566 of 2000 on the next day i.e. 19.10.2000. 

 4. Respondent No.2 also filed Family Suit No. 221 of 2000 on 24.8.2000 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court and Family Court, Dhaka under Section 5(Gha) of the Family Courts Ordinance praying for guardianship and custody of Syed Afzal Amin stating inter alia that (a) she left the house of the Petitioner for reasons of incompatibility, and (b) that the Petitioner is unable to look after the minor. 

 5. It is the contention of the Petitioner that he put in an appearance in the said Family Suit on 24.9.2000 and the Learned Court fixed 1.10.2000 for submission of written statements and written objection. The Petitioner contends further that in the meantime the Petitioner and Respondent No.2 having made concerted efforts towards a possible rapprochement and the Respondent No.2 having verbally assured the Petitioner of amicably settling out of Court the outstanding issues as constituted the subject-matter of the said Family Suit, the Petitioner was misled thereby in not contesting the Suit. It so transpired, however, that the Respondent No.1 Senior Assistant Judge by an Order dated 10.10.2000 fixed 18.10.2000 for the hearing of the Suit. It is the Petitioner's contention that on the date so assigned for hearing, being also the date on which the Compromise Deed , Annexure —`B' was executed between the Petitioner and Respondent No.2, Respondent No.2 surreptitiously and beyond the knowledge of the Petitioner examined herself as P.W. 1 and the Court ultimately fixed 26.10.2000 for arguments. On 26.10.2000 Respondent No.1 partially allowed the application of the Respondent No.2 and by way of the Impugned Order appointed Respondent No.2 as guardian of the minor boy Syed Afzal Amin (Annexure-'D'). 

 6. This Impugned Order, passed ex-parte during the subsistence of the Petitioner's marriage to Respondent No.2, denying the Petitioner the guardianship of his minor son was followed nearly two years later by the issuance of a notice dated 10.7.2002 at the in-stance of the Respondent No.2 issued under the relevant provisions of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 for the dissolution of her marriage to the Petitioner. This Court notes that it is the Petitioner's admitted position that Section 17(3) of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985 provides for an appeal from the judgment and order of a Family Court to the Court of District. Judge prescribing a 30-day period from the date of such judgment and order within which such appeal must be preferred. It is the Petitioner's contention that having remained oblivious of the fact, nature and extent of the Impugned Order dated 26.10.2000 until a much later date when this 

 Impugned Order except in moving this Court in Writ Jurisdiction. 

 8. It is in this regard that the Learned Counsel for the Petitioner, Mr. Ozair Farook submits that the Respondent No.1 Family Court erred in law in appointing Respondent No.2 as the guardian of the minor boy without assigning any cogent and legally tenable reason for ascribing or imputing to the Petitioner undetermined degree of incapacity thereby negating his status as a natural guardian Of the minor. 

 9. In light of the above this Court is therefore asked to find on matters of both this 

 Court's jurisdiction to entertain this Writ, and once that hurdle is overcome, on the legality 

 and validity of the Impugned Order. It appears to this Court that consideration of both matters are somewhat coextensive and in this regard this Court notes Mr. Ozair Farook's submission that the Respondent No.1 Court in an ostensible assumption of authority under Section 19 of The Guardians and Wards Act 1890, (a) accorded to itself jurisdiction by a wrong decision on matters that it is empowered only to enquire and determine the extent of its jurisdiction, and moreover (b)in the process of giving a wrong decision gave it in a manner not in compliance with the specific requirements of Section 19 of the Act. The relevant portions of Section 19 of the Act 

 "Nothing in this Chapter shall authorise the Court to appoint or declare a guardian 

 of a minor whose property is under the superintendence of a Court of Wards, or to appoint or declare a guardian of the person - 

 (b) of a minor whose father is living, and is not, in the opinion of the Court, unfit to be guardian of the person of the minor... 

 10. Reading the Impugned Order in light of Section 19 it is evident that the Respondent No.1 Court in granting the application of the Respondent No.2 for guardianship of her son has done so by summarily deciding on the existence of facts as spelt out in the application. That application dated 18.10.2000 (Annexure-'C') sets out the Petitioner's abusive behaviour towards the Respondent No.2 as has generated fear in their minor son towards the Petitioner as the ground for granting the Respondent No.2 the minor's guardianship. This Court notes that the Impugned Order by oblique reference and not by express enunciation has found this ground sufficient to justify the granting of the guardianship of the minor to the Respondent No. 2. 

 11. On a plain reading of Section 19 of the Act this Court finds it primarily declaratory of a lack of authority and jurisdiction of a court to appoint a guardian of a person of a minor during the lifetime of the father. In other words, it is incumbent upon a court to ascertain in the first instance the fact of a father's existence and of his incapacities, if any, to be a guardian of the person of the minor, special facts and circumstances upon which the limits of that court's jurisdiction depends. A proper assessment of those facts is not reflected in the Impugned Order. Instead that process has been supplanted by a decision allowing guardianship apparently by way of a wrong reading of those facts. In arguing for this Court's authority to assume jurisdiction in such instances Mr. Ozair Farook refers to the following observation by Lord Goddard in R. v. Fulham (etc.) Rent Tribunal ex parte Zerek (U9511) 2KB 1,6): 

 .. if a certain state of things has to exist before an inferior tribunal have jurisdiction, they can inquire into the facts in order to decide whether or not they have jurisdiction, but cannot give themselves jurisdiction by a wrong decision upon them; and this Court may, by means of proceeding for certiorari, inquire into the correctness of the decision." 

 This view has been endorsed subsequently, for example, in the case of M/s Reza Textiles Ltd. v. Income Tax Officer, Rampur reported in AIR 1973 Supreme Court 1362 at 1363 thus: 

 "No authority ... can confer jurisdiction on itself by deciding a jurisdictional fact wrongly. The question whether the jurisdictional fact has been rightly decided or not is a question that is open for examination by the High Court in an application for a writ of certiorari." On the basis of these dicta this Court holds that this Court will find jurisdiction in such cases especially where the Petitioner has no other efficacious remedy available to him. 

 12. This Court is of the view that the primary factor limiting the Respondent No.1 Court's jurisdiction in appointing Respondent No.2 as guardian is a general prohibition of such appointment in Section 19(b) of the Act, taking place during the lifetime of a minor's father. 

 13. Learned Counsel for the Respondent No.2, Ms. Sigma Huda has submitted that the Respondent No.1 Court having acted primarily in the interest of the welfare of the minor in this case, that in itself would validate the assumption of jurisdiction by the Respondent No. 1 Court. In this regard Ms. Huda has referred to Section 17 of the Act in particular. Section 17 insofar it is relevant reads thus: 

 "17(1). In appointing or declaring the guardian of a minor, the Court shall, subject to the provisions of this section, be guided by what ... appears in the circumstances to be for the welfare of the minor." 

 "... in the case of a minor whose father is living there and is not in the opinion of the court unfit to be guardian of the person of the minor, no guardian can be appointed. When therefore, Section 17 lays down that in appointing or declaring the guardian of a minor, the court shall be guided by what appears in the circumstances to be for the welfare of the minor, it does not mean that Section 17 overrides Section 19. Only if the father is unfit to be the guardian, can the question of the welfare of the minor come into consideration. In other words, under Section 17, there is no question of a guardian of his person being appointed if the father is alive and is not unfit to be the guardian. The father is entitled to be the guardian even as against the mother as long as he is not held to be unfit to be the guardian of the person of his son." Acting upon a long 

 15. In other words, the legal assumption here is that a father is best placed in securing the minor's welfare by way of managing and supervising the minor's affairs. This is what the notion of a father's guardianship encapsulates in its totality. The inability of the Respondent No. 1 Court to appreciate the legal recognition of a father's naturally protective role as a guardian as clearly evident in the Impugned Order has resulted in what Hamoodur Rahman, J held in the case of Khizar Hayat Khan v. Zainab Begum reported in 19 DLR (SC) 1967, 372, at page 379 as an usurpation of jurisdiction it does not possess both on an erroneous view of the law and an erroneous assumption of fact. Accordingly, and in view of long standing and established authority having clearly subjected such assumption of jurisdiction to this Court's review and scrutiny, this Court finds no reason to deviate from the same in the instant case not-withstanding the Petitioner not having availed of the appeal provisions of the Act. 

 16. The supremacy of the Petitioner's natural guardianship so established under Section 19 of the Act this Court is now asked to examine the extent to which the Impugned Order stands vitiated by failure to cite cogent and legally tenable- reasons for denying the Petitioner his right of natural guardianship. It is this Court's view that the statutory protection attached to the natural guardianship of a father and its attendant legal implications is not summarily dislodged in the manner done under the Impugned Order. Crucial to any process of dislodgement as sanctioned in Section 19(b) is the Court's express finding of the father's incapacity. That is in turn premised on a Court's satisfaction of facts of incapacity pleaded and established like any other fact by evidence. There is nothing in the Impugned Order to show that that exercise has been undertaken in this case.
